Raw_Evidence_Span: Section 3.2: Boundary layer model, stationary crack analysis

Composition.Note: E = 210 GPa, ν = 0.3, D = 0.0127 mm²/s, V_H = 2000 mm³/mol

Simulation_Metadata.Element_Type: Quadratic plane strain quadrilateral elements with reduced integration

Mesh_Params.Refinement: Mesh refined along crack propagation region

Governing_Equations: Chemical potential with hydrostatic stress coupling (Eq. 13)

Key_Model_Parameters.Initial_Condition: Pre-charged: C(t=0) = C0 = 0.5 wt ppm uniformly

Simulation_Metadata.Boundary_Conditions: Remote KI field applied via Williams expansion displacements on outer boundary; hydrogen concentration C_env at boundaries
Simulation_Metadata.Original_Values: E = 210 GPa, ν = 0.3, D = 0.0127 mm²/s, VH = 2000 mm³/mol, C0 = 0.5 wt ppm, ΔK = 1 MPa√m, f = 1 Hz, R = 0

Structure_Text.original: Boundary layer model: circular domain with sharp crack, upper half modeled due to symmetry; stationary and propagating crack analyses
Structure_Text.simplified: Boundary layer formulation for small scale yielding; cracked circular domain under remote KI

Advanced_Quantitative_Features.Geometry: Circular domain, upper half (symmetry), with sharp crack
Advanced_Quantitative_Features.Normalization: C/C0 = F(f_bar, t_bar, E*V_H/RT) per Buckingham Pi theorem

Properties.Note: Fig. 5: C/C0 ahead of stationary crack tip at Kmax, Km, Kmin stages of first load cycle under steady state. Hydrogen concentration increases with applied load, maximum near crack tip. Visual data not extracted.

Fig. 6: Time evolution of C/C0 at r/L0 ≈ 0.2×10^7 ahead of crack tip for various loading frequencies. At high f (10^3 Hz), concentration flattens ~5% below max at low frequencies. Visual data not extracted.

Structure_Text.simplified: Boundary layer model for Paris law analysis and frequency regime mapping

Properties.Note: Fig. 7: Normalized crack extension vs. N for different C_env. Higher hydrogen concentration leads to larger crack extension. Visual data not extracted.
Properties.Trend: For a given number of cycles, higher hydrogen concentration yields larger crack extension

Properties.Note: Fig. 8: da/dN vs. ΔK on log-log scale for different C_env. Paris regime is linear; Paris coefficient C increases with hydrogen content; Paris exponent m ≈ 3.2, relatively insensitive to environment.
Properties.Paris_Exponent_m_Note: Approximately 3.2; within range reported for metals in inert environments
Properties.Trend: Paris coefficient C increases with hydrogen content; Paris exponent m appears less sensitive to environment

Properties.Note: Fig. 9: da/dN vs. normalized frequency f_bar = f*L0^2/D for ΔK/K0 = 0.24, R = 0, C0 = C_env = 0.1 wt ppm. Two limiting regimes captured: high f (diminished embrittlement) and low f (maximum embrittlement) with smooth transition.
Properties.Trend: Crack growth rate sensitive to loading frequency; two limit states captured with smooth transition

Structure_Text.original: Cylindrical bar with a circumferential notch on its surface; axisymmetric conditions exploited; phase field and hydrogen concentration contours showing crack growth and environmental exposure
Structure_Text.simplified: Notched cylindrical bar under cyclic loading with hydrogen; axisymmetric model

Properties.Note: Fig. 11: Virtual S-N curves for notched bar at C_env = 0.1, 0.5, 1 wt ppm. Shorter fatigue lives with higher hydrogen content. Slope of S-N curve appears insensitive to hydrogen content. Visual data not extracted.
